result.rule: Model every distinct activity, event, participant, decision, branch, loop, message and outcome stated in the description. Do not invent process facts.
Use start events for stated process triggers. A start event has no incoming sequence flow and is not the source of a message flow.
Do not merge separately described actions into one task or split one stated action without a process reason. Preserve described dependencies.
Distinguish message tasks from message events: a task models performed work; an event models a message occurrence affecting flow.
A white-box participant references its process with processRef. A black-box participant has no processRef and no modeled internal workflow.
Allow multiple start or end events when the description has distinct triggers or outcomes. Do not force all outcomes into one end.

result.rule: When the description says that a participant performs an action that initiates the process: Model the process trigger with a start event, then model the participant’s described action as a distinct task; do not use the action itself as the start event.

When the description presents receipt of a physical item as a process step, rather than explicitly describing a wait for a message, signal, time, or condition.: Model the receipt as a task, not an intermediate catch event.
When the description states an occurrence that starts the process: Label the start event with a concise phrase naming that trigger rather than a generic label.

When the description distinguishes an action that occurs before a later recording, confirmation, or other outcome: Model that action as a distinct activity in the sequence; do not omit it or use a terminal outcome event as its substitute.

args.text: When a process description states an outcome or activity, use BPMN labels that faithfully represent that stated meaning; do not add an outcome that the description does not specify.

trace.reason: Check whether documented guidance already addresses faithful and evidence-based element labels.

result.rule: When the description does not justify a specialized construct, use the simplest compatible BPMN construct and do not guess missing semantics.
Model every distinct activity, event, participant, decision, branch, loop, message and outcome stated in the description. Do not invent process facts.
Use short, faithful labels in the input language. Prefer verb-object activity names and meaningful business triggers or outcomes for events.
Represent each modeled internal workflow with bpmn:process. Use isExecutable=false unless execution-ready behavior is explicitly required and fully specified.
Return one complete, well-formed bpmn:definitions document and no surrounding explanation or Markdown fence.
Create reusable bpmn:message elements and messageRef only when communication content or shared message identity matters.

args.text: When labeling BPMN activities and events, preserve the meaning stated in the process description; do not label an event with an outcome that the description does not specify.

trace.reason: Check whether an error-driven guideline already covers faithful labels and unsupported event outcomes.

result.rule: When the description distinguishes a process trigger, an activity, or an outcome from other stages of the process: Label each BPMN element according to the meaning of its corresponding described trigger, activity, or outcome; do not substitute a different stage or its purpose or result.
When the description specifies an activity’s object, recipient, or other meaningful qualifier: Preserve that qualifier in the BPMN task label rather than replacing it with a broader paraphrase.

When the description distinguishes an event or activity by its action, actor, object, recipient, or another meaningful qualifier: Label each BPMN element so that it preserves those stated details without substituting a broader or different meaning.

When the description gives an activity together with contextual or explanatory details that are not needed to distinguish the activity in its process context: Label the BPMN task with its core action and necessary object, omitting redundant contextual modifiers while preserving details essential to the activity’s meaning.
